lines.watchItem: Merchant-GPU demand still runs far ahead of what the chain can build, with the leading vendor guiding next-year growth near 70 percent while customer forecasts imply about double that. Wafer-start planning sits against a demand signal that measures the shortfall rather than the appetite, and the pacing items are construction labour and tool delivery.

Advanced-packaging allocation is again named the limit on how many AI systems reach customers, with quoted waits of roughly 52 to 78 weeks and capacity around 105,000 to 130,000 wafers a month by the end of this year. Realizable accelerator revenue is exposed to how fast that gap closes rather than to order intake.

Advanced-packaging output is booked by very few buyers, with more than 85 percent pre-booked and one customer reserving roughly 800,000 to 850,000 wafers of this year's capacity. The exposure is that a single buyer trimming orders would leave slots that are slow to refill.

Custom accelerators are becoming a larger share of leading-node work, with one design house reporting AI chip sales of $16.7 billion in a quarter and pointing to far more by fiscal 2028, while a model lab and a large cloud both put their own parts into leading-edge production. The leading-node customer base is tilting from merchant GPU vendors toward buyers who design their own silicon.

Memory cost is moving through the chain into finished prices, with the leading vendor raising AI server prices by more than 15 percent and still guiding its own margin down toward the low 70s. The second-largest foundry has already raised new-order prices 10 to 15 percent, so firm pricing across the chain is currently a memory-cost story as much as a demand story.

A rival packaging route is winning committed volume, with more than three million bridge-packaging units ordered for a 2028 cloud accelerator and reported yields above 90 percent at about half the cost of the incumbent method. That route still holds a small share of 2.5D capacity and carries its own single-supplier choke point, so the watch is on whether committed volume actually moves.

Washington is preparing chip tariffs that would reach finished data-centre servers, with duty-free allowances sized to each company's US fabrication investment and no rate or start date set. US capacity commitments now carry a policy value beyond their output, which cuts both ways until the rule is written.

One model lab has signed about $517 billion of compute agreements in eleven months against roughly $180 billion of spending it had guided investors toward, with the commitments resting on money it has not yet raised. A slice of the forward order book therefore depends on capital markets staying open to buyers who are not yet profitable.
